newsitem.title: USA: Busy factories, policy-makers' hints fan rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Busy factories, policy-makers' hints fan rate fears.

text.p: Strong February factory orders reported Wednesday added to signs of an accelerating economy as Federal Reserve policy-makers hinted at more interest-rate increases and sent stock prices plummeting anew.
New orders at factory gates rose by 0.8 percent in February to a seasonally adjusted record $325.9 billion after a 2.5 percent surge in January business, the Commerce Department said.
Shipments of finished products picked up, order backlogs fattened and inventories were built up from January in apparent anticipation of brisk demand.

Coupled with earlier remarks by Federal Reserve Gov. Laurence Meyer that the economy was showing profound strength, the report helped to grease another huge slide in stock prices on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Dow Jones industrial average plunged more than 100 points by midday as its downward trend since late last week was unabated. In late trading the Dow was off 99 points at 6,512.
"The economy is really strong," Meyer told The Washington Post. "This is not a fluke."

Just a week ago, Fed policy-makers, including Meyer, decided to push up short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point due to concerns that vigorous consumer spending risked igniting inflationary wage and price rises.

A Fed official, in a telephone interview with Reuters, suggested higher real interest rates might be needed to brake growth. But the official said a steep rise comparable to that initiated in seven stages in 1994 and early 1995 when rates were moved up three percentage points was unlikely.

"There's no reason to believe rates are going to march up by percentage points in the next six months," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. He noted that the Fed would be more comfortable with economic growth in its target zone of 2 percent to 2-1/4 percent instead of at current robust levels.

Meyer declined to comment directly on what the Fed might do at its next meeting May 20. But financial markets have been rattled by speculation that a series of rate rises may be needed to slowly collar demand by boosting borrowing charges.

A closely watched report on Tuesday showing that a key index compiled by the National Association of Purchasing Management hit a two-year peak in March bolstered the impression that the economy may accelerate in the spring rather than slow as the Fed wants.

"The bad news that we're seeing is that, given the forward momentum the economy had in the first two months, together with the little peek we've had at March, all the data ahead may be coming in strong," said economist Sam Kahan of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd. in Chicago.

"What we're seeing so far points to real first-quarter GDP (gross domestic product) growth of 3.5 percent, possibly higher," Kahan said, after a 3.8 percent annual rate of increase in national output in last year's fourth quarter.
Moreover, the current economic vigour appears to be coming from different sources than was the case last year, when much of the growth was from production for inventories.

"There's been a shift in the areas of strength toward consumption, which tends to be more long-lasting," Kahan said, since consumer spending fuels two-thirds of national economic activity and it is being fanned by steady job and income gains.
The Fed official similarly noted "very strong" consumption. "Generally out there, there seems to be optimistic business, optimistic consumers and an ample supply of credit," the official said.
The Commerce Department said factory business intensified in February for both costly durables and more quickly used nondurables like food and paper items.
Orders for expensive durables like refrigerators and manufacturing machinery intended to last three years or more, grew by 1.5 percent to $177.9 billion after a 3.8 percent rise in January.
Non-durable products posted a 0.1 percent increase following a 0.9 percent rise in January.

But orders for transportation goods -- the largest single category in terms of value -- fell in February by 4.1 percent to $40.6 billion after a 1.5 percent rise in January. Orders were weaker for new cars, airplanes and other goods aside from railroad equipment.
Excluding transportation, factory orders rose in February by 1.6 percent after a 2.6 percent increase in January.
